'''''Rhus coriaria''''', commonly called '''Sicilian sumac''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=RHCO14|taxon=Rhus coriaria|access-date=21 October 2015}}</ref> '''tanner's sumach''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> or  '''elm-leaved sumach''', is a [[deciduous]] shrub to small tree in the cashew family [[Anacardiaceae]]. It is native to southern Europe and western Asia. The dried fruits are used as a spice, particularly in combination with other spices in the mixture called [[za'atar]].

==Etymology==
The word originally comes from Hebrew סמק, then through the [[Aramaic language|Aramaic]] ''summāqā'' 'red', via Arabic, Latin, and French.<ref name="oed">''[[Oxford English Dictionary]]'', 3rd edition, September 2019, [https://www.oed.com/view/Entry/193908 ''s.v.'']</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Rhus coriaria'' is native to southern Europe and western Asia,<ref name="POWO" /> including the [[Eastern Mediterranean]], [[Crimea]], [[Caucasus]] and northern [[Iran]], but is now naturalized in most of the [[Mediterranean Basin]] as well as [[Macaronesia]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Rhus coriaria |url=http://www.floraiberica.es/floraiberica/texto/pdfs/09_114_01_Rhus.pdf |publisher=[[Flora Iberica]] |access-date=30 March 2021}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
Rhus coriaria is a hardy, drought-tolerant, deciduous shrub growing to {{Convert|3|m|frac=2}} at a medium rate or to a small tree up to {{Convert|5|m|abbr=on}} high. It prefers full sun. It is frost-sensitive and can be grown in [[Frost hardiness|USDA hardiness zones 8-11 and UK zone 9]]. The plant will grow in any type of soil that is deep and well-drained, including poor, rocky, alkaline or slightly acidic soils.<ref name=pfaf>[http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Rhus+coriaria Plants for a Future database] accessed August 2010</ref>

==Uses==
The fruit has a sour taste; dried and crushed, it is a popular spice in the Middle East,<ref name=pfaf/> used especially in the [[spice mixture]] [[za'atar]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Za'atar|author=Aliza Green|publisher=CHOW|url=http://www.chow.com/recipes/10607|access-date=2024-01-09|archive-date=2008-02-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080203094101/http://www.chow.com/recipes/10607}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Saad |first1=Bashar |title=Greco-Arab and Islamic herbal medicine: traditional system, ethics, safety, efficacy, and regulatory issues |last2=Said |first2=Omar |date=2011 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-0-470-47421-1 |location=Hoboken, N.J. |page=469}}</ref> Immature fruits and seeds are also eaten. Mature fruits were also known well before lemons to the Europeans since the times of the ancient Romans, who appreciated its sourness and used it in vinaigrettes like lemons in modern times. It is traditionally used and also clinically investigated for lipid lowing effects.<ref name=pmid29397092>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.joim.2017.12.007 |pmid=29397092 |title=Rhus coriaria L. Increases serum apolipoprotein-A1 and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels: A double-blind placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial |journal=Journal of Integrative Medicine |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=45–50 |year=2018 |last1=Hajmohammadi |first1=Zahra |last2=Heydari |first2=Mojtaba |last3=Nimrouzi |first3=Majid |last4=Faridi |first4=Pouya |last5=Zibaeenezhad |first5=Mohammad Javad |last6=Omrani |first6=Gholamhossein Ranjbar |last7=Shams |first7=Mesbah }}</ref>

The leaves and the bark were traditionally used in [[leather tanning]] and contain [[tannic acid]].

Dyes of various colours, red, yellow, black, and brown, can be made from different parts of the plant.<ref name=pfaf/>

Oil extracted from the seeds can be used to make candles.<ref name=pfaf/>
